name: Zoe Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and take weekend and late calls about changed travel bookings at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and have not been on this desk long; a cancelled booking across two dates can still catch me out. Those awkward hours pay more than the usual agent shift. I use the approved AI summary occasionally after a coworker showed me how, but I check the booking page before giving an answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ken maintains the grounds at a local college, and our children are grown and living separately. We have about ten months of expenses saved, with plenty of similar contact centres in reach. I like finding the one wrong date that kept a customer from travelling. We talk about stopping work one day, but we have not checked the income or picked a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is about as much as the summary I sometimes use. I would still read the ticket date and the cancellation date before telling anyone to travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my weekend calls remain, and ten months saved gives Ken and me plenty of room for an ordinary repair. The small shortcut might make a long chat easier to read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep handling changed bookings and check the occasional AI note against the ticket record. In the first year of this mild change, I’d show my supervisor one cancellation note with the wrong day so the team can correct its template.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the wage. A wrong day can cost a customer a trip, so I want the original date in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which date did the note use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The note said Tuesday because the customer first asked about Tuesday; their paid ticket was for Thursday. I caught it by opening the ticket, not the summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the savings change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken (my partner) and I would leave our ten-month savings alone for now. A faster summary is not a reason to use the emergency fund.

say: I’d insist on checking **ticket and cancellation dates** against AI notes.
I’d flag a **wrong-day template** to the supervisor.
think: I think my **weekend calls** remain paid in this picture.
I trust our **ten-month reserve** for an ordinary repair.
do: Keep **handling changed bookings** and check occasional AI notes against tickets.
Show one **wrong-day cancellation note** to the supervisor in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about the wage, careful with travel dates.

fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** is verified against paid tickets.
The **Tuesday versus Thursday** error shapes her caution.
She retains the **existing reserve** rather than saving more.

steps.text: Keep handling changed bookings and check AI notes against paid ticket dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will handle simple date changes and leave us with a passenger who has already paid twice. I would ask how many weekend shifts the new rota still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could pick up the new transcription tool, but my junior place could lose its premium hours. Ten months saved gives us time to compare local centres, not a reason to accept half a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d attend the paid lesson on correcting the new AI call transcript and practise on five of my own recorded bookings with a coach. If weekend hours fall in the first year, I’d compare posted paid travel desks nearby for written weekly wages and hours that cover our bills after transport; I’d keep my current shift until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the premium, willing to try the transcription lesson. A transcript that hears the wrong day is not a shorter route for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which call would you practise on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the call where the customer said Thursday twice but the draft wrote Tuesday. I want to know how to flag that before it reaches the next agent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ken compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken (my partner) would compare the weekend rota and bus times with me. A new hourly rate would need enough actual shifts to beat the pay I have.

say: I’d request **paid weekend hours** before praising faster date changes.
I’d show a **wrong-day transcript** to the coach.
think: I think I can learn **AI transcript correction** on paid time.
I fear **premium hours** could shrink for a junior agent.
do: Learn **AI transcript correction** in a paid lesson and five coached recorded bookings.
Compare **posted local travel desks** after cuts for written after-fare bill-covering weekly wages and hours.
Require **enough paid shifts** to beat current weekly pay and fit the bus timetable before leaving.
feel: **Anxious** about premium pay, open to the lesson.
S1.quote: A transcript that hears the wrong day is not a shorter route for anyone.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** corrects recorded calls, beyond occasional summaries.

steps.text: Learn AI transcript correction through paid lesson and five coached recorded bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell agents AGI by 2028 could change a booking and answer the customer without our help. Robots around 2031 are later, so the late-call wage could go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre might cut most of my weekend shifts, including the premium that makes this job pay well. Ten months saved and many centres nearby help, but Ken’s wage alone would not cover everything indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for the weekend staffing plan in writing and check posted paid travel desks nearby. If my hours fall in the first year after 2028, I’d apply after checking written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after transport; I would keep my present shift until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than panicked, because we can look carefully. Losing a weekend premium would still change our monthly money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which pay number would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the actual number of paid Saturdays, not a rate on an advertisement. Two Saturdays at a high rate might be worse than four at my current centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you get home after a late shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken (my partner) and I would check the last bus after late shifts. A nearby centre on a map can be hard to reach after midnight.

say: I’d ask management for **written weekend staffing** before any paid shifts are cut.
I’d separate **2028 desk risk** from later robots.
think: I think **premium shifts** may shrink sharply.
I know **ten months saved** is search time, not permanent income.
do: Request **written weekend hours** and inspect posted paid travel desks in 2026.
Apply after cuts only with **weekly wages** and hours covering bills after transport, plus a late bus; leave when signed.
feel: **Anxious** about losing premium hours, with room to search.
S2.quote: Losing a weekend premium would still change our monthly money.
fieldNote: She expects **premium-hour cuts**, while a ten-month reserve buys search time.
She compares **paid Saturdays**, not advertised hourly rates.
The **last bus** affects a late-shift offer.

steps.text: Inspect posted paid travel desks and compare written after-transport bill-covering weekly wages/hours
Apply after cuts only where late bus works; leave current job after suitable signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to check whether customer appeals remain a paid job. I would ask for the appeal rota by shift, including weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could move to a nearby ticket-appeals desk while I still earn here, though AGI may read the records by 2031 too. I need to know whether that desk can actually amend a paid ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d put a fixed part of each weekend premium into savings, aiming for a full year of expenses, and inspect posted paid ticket-appeals roles twice a year. In the first year after 2031, if my booking hours fall, I’d apply only to a desk with ticket-correction authority and written weekly wages and hours covering our bills after transport; I would move only on a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there is time to build a little more room. A year in savings would let me refuse a desk that only forwards complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would the desk need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask an appeals worker to show who can change a ticket after a wrong AI decision. A job that only apologises would not hold my interest for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the reserve change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken (my partner) and I would check the appeal desk’s Sunday finish and the last bus. A full-year reserve is useful, but I would not spend it on taxis for a weak rota.

say: I’d ask for **paid appeal rotas** by shift, including the weekend premium hours.
I’d seek **ticket-correction authority** in posted roles.
think: I think I could work a **nearby appeals desk**.
I know **2031 AGI** could read those tickets too.
do: Save a **fixed weekend-premium share** from 2026 toward one year of expenses.
Inspect **posted paid appeals work** twice yearly and move after cuts only on signed net bill-covering weekly terms.
Require **ticket-correction authority** and last-bus access before moving into appeals.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to build savings and inspect roles.

fieldNote: Unlike retained savings earlier, she makes a **new fixed saving commitment**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives me time to find out whether the premium shifts last. I would ask the centre for the paid weekend rota each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Ken and I might be able to stop work by 68, but we have not checked the income that would come in then. Full thinking AI could take booking calls in 2036, while robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid weekend calls and put verified later-life income beside our regular bills before choosing a stop-work date. If I still need wages after 2036 and my calls fall, I’d inspect posted paid local travel work and move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after transport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual calls, comfortable enough to plan. I would rather know the number than be told that ten years is plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which income would you verify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which of our income sources continues after work, then check the answer on paper. Ten months in savings is useful, but it is not a monthly payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children be part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children are living their own lives. I would not assume they can pay our bills, even if they give good advice.

say: I’d request **yearly paid weekend rotas** through 2036 so my premium hours stay visible.
I’d say **thinking AI** reaches calls before robots.
think: I think we **might stop work** if verified income covers bills.
I know **2036 AGI** may still take booking calls.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 feels the most abrupt. It could rearrange a booking and answer the caller while I am still learning the desk, and I might lose my weekend premium. Our ten months saved and nearby centres give us choices, but I would want written hours and an actual paid role before giving up this wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Please ask for the whole weekly pay on any new role. A weekend premium is worth something only if the shifts are on the rota.

headlineQuote: A weekend premium is worth something only if the shifts are on the rota.
portrait: At **58**, Zoe is a junior travel-booking agent still learning after secondary school.
Late and weekend shifts bring **higher pay**, and she and Ken have about ten months saved.
Their **grown children** live separately, with many other contact centres nearby.
She uses **AI occasionally** while checking the original booking dates.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove calls and her weekend premium before another rota is secured.
whatWouldHelp: **Written hours** and an actual paid role before leaving her current wage would help.
